short: Mutinous imperial troops wrecked Rome and ended its High Renaissance.
full:
On 6 May 1527 an unpaid imperial army of some 20,000 Spanish, Italian and German troops, many of the Landsknechte Lutheran, stormed the walls of Rome. Their commander, Charles de Bourbon, was shot dead in the assault, leaving the force with no one able to control it. Pope Clement VII, who had joined the League of Cognac against Charles V, escaped along the Passetto di Borgo to the Castel Sant'Angelo. Of the 189 Swiss Guards who covered the retreat at St Peter's, 42 survived.

The city was pillaged for months. Churches were stripped, archives and libraries destroyed, and the population fell from around 55,000 to perhaps a fifth of that through killing, flight and plague. The last imperial troops marched out in February 1528. Clement had already capitulated. The sack ended Rome's High Renaissance as a working artistic centre and confirmed Habsburg dominance in Italy; the Swiss Guard still swears in recruits on 6 May. Sabaton's "The Last Stand" (2016) is about the guardsmen.
